Bone chilling

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A new report on the lion bone industry exposes just how the department is enabling the cruel killing of our lions for profit

Unique Selling Point:
Hi profile good interviews, and hopefully good confrontations

Summary:
Only 20 000 wild lions remain across the entire African continent. An estimated 8000 of those lions are unashamedly exploited for profit in a cruel and hidden multimillion dollar business right under our noses in the Free State and the North West province.

Carte Blanche first exposed the canned hunting business to South Africans in 1997. Twenty years later that industry has given way to a darker, crueler industry - the trading of thousands of lion skeletons, by farmers, Chinese middlemen and exporters and enabled by the DEA, under the leadership of Edna Molewa.

In 2017, the South African Government issued an export quota of 800 lion skeletons from captive bred lions, but our sources have told us that thousands more are being exported to Vietnam, China and Laos. By making the trade in lion bones legal, the illegal trade is made easier.



Further information:
South Africa is now the world's largest legal exporter of lion bones and skeletons. Between 2008 and 2015, the country declared exports of more than 5,000 lion skeletons and a large quantity of bones. The buyers and countries to which these products are destined have strong associations with wildlife trafficking.

In a new report we track the associations between notorious rhino horn and wildlife smugglers and the lion bone industry and also show an association between this industry and the burgeoning donkey skin industry.

According to written answers to questions in parliament, the first legal trade in lion bones and skeleton from South Africa began in 2008 when lion bones began to be used as a substitute for tiger bones in expensive fortifying "wine" and other medicinal products in some Far Eastern communities. Lion bones are sometimes substituted for tiger bones without the knowledge of users.

The DEA has repeatedly stated that it believes the breeding of lions in captivity for hunting and trade in skeletons and bones, as a byproduct of hunting, is compatible with the concept of promoting the "Green Economy". However, it acknowledges that it is unable to demonstrate any conservation value from captive lion breeding. The department also acknowledges that it has no scientific evidence to demonstrate that the trade in bones from captive-bred lions will in fact protect wild lions in Africa or tigers in Asia.

Several people well connected within the South African hunting industry have indicated in recent interviews with researchers that the price at "the breeding-farm gate" had increased significantly and R30,000 - R50,000 a skeleton is now the going price depending on the size.

"The prices have increased a lot since 2013 and some guys are making big money, particularly if the skeleton comes from a lion that someone has already paid to hunt," one professional hunter, who asked not to be named in this report, said during an interview with a researcher. "A trader will pay R50,000 for a big male skeleton with its skull, teeth and claws."

So where do the bones go and who is driving the trade? Carte Blanche goes to those named in the report for comment, speaks to international conservation figure Will Travers, the hunters condemning the trade and the Minister of Tourism Mr Derek Hanekom. We also take on the Minister of Environment Edna Molewa whose department is enabling this shocking practice.

Bone Chilling FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 8th APRIL 2018

Commentary One
This cub, removed from its mother soon after its born, is one of around 7000 lions in 200 lion breeding farms across the free state, Limpopo and North West

Up sound lion yawns

This is the face of the captive bred lion industry. It will be bottle fed, petted, grow up and shot.

Up sound gunshot

Volunteers pay foreign currency to raise it, tourists pay to pet it. It will be hunted,or executed for its bones. Its skeleton will be bought by bone agents and sold to China, Vietnam or Laos, to be used for a wine that has no medicinal value

Will Travers
Our view here is that it is about cash before conservation.

Commentary Two
Recently John Webb met with Will Travers in London. He's president of the Born Free Foundation and they have just released this report on captive bred lions.

Will Travers
Captive breeding is unique to South Africa, it doesn't happen in any other country and its shameful in that respect. It's all about money

Commentary Three
Travers's ties to African lions goes back to the sixties, when his parents Virginia Mckenna and Bill Travers were the stars of Born Free, the story of George and Joy Adamson and Elsa the Lion.

Up sound movie

Commentary Four
Now 50 years later the Born Free Foundation is calling for an end to captive bred lions for hunting, and to stop a newer, second income stream for the lion breeders - raising the lions only to kill them for their bones - worth up to R50 000 per skeleton.

Will Travers
Laos has an import quota of 10 tonnes of lion bones recently, if the illegal trade takes off then I see that as the tipping point for Africa's lion populations

Commentary Five
The Born Free report takes aim at the appointed custodian of our wildlife, Minister Edna Molewa, who in June last year, legalized the export of 800 lion skeletons annually. Her policies promote the hunting of hand raised lions while effectively leaving the welfare of the animals to the very people who slaughter them

WILL TRAVERS
I have met minister Molewa on several occasions., I have asked to meet her and see if there is a way forward that is humane and inclusive and despite her saying on each occasion absolutely lets meet, since 2012, 2013 we have not been able to make that meeting

Commentary Six
In the meantime, farmers have cashed in, and this brutal industry is raking in millions.

Paul Stones
The DEA is not going to turn around tomorrow and say we are going to stop the captive bred lion industry. The DEA is 100% responsible for why it is there in the first place!

Commentary seven
In November last year Professional Hunter Paul Stones and other hunters, concerned about the ethics of hunting captive bred lions, turned their backs on their former hunting association- PHASA. Captive bred lion hunting, had finally split the hunting industry down the middle

Up sound hunter

Paul Stones
Bred as cubs, taken into pens, catalogue sold, shot on properties 3 4 5 days, which is what some of them are doing now.

Commentary eight
Their new hunting association, the Custodians of Professional Hunters reject any form of captive lion hunting

Paul Stones
We always hoped that PHASA would see the light - it was a practice we could not justify, condemned by everyone in the hunting world

Commentary nine
Internationally it's also changing. In February, Safari Club international's 50 000 hunters also slammed the door on captive bred lion hunters, refusing to recognize their trophy's or allow the lion breeders to advertise at their shows.

Will Travers
I think Brand South Africa is under the spotlight, the 9 plus million tourists may start to rethink their attitude towards South Africa's credentials for conservation, maybe with the change of leadership there is an opportunity for President Ramaphosa to now say, I want to look at this again

Commentary ten
But at PHASA, the professional hunters of SA, they're standing firm in defence of captive bred hunting. Spokesman Richard York

Derek
Are you aware of the image of SA when it comes to hunting associations and bodies like born Free?
Richard York
Yes, we are aware
Derek
What is that image of South Africa?
Richard
The image of South Africa is being portrayed negatively by certain journalistic viewpoints. All the articles mention canned hunting where we as PHASA are opposed to canned hunting, but the journalists can't avoid not using that sensationalistic word play.

Commentary eleven
PHASA says hunted lions should not be bottle fed, and must be released for at least a month before they are hunted

Richard
We have 7000 lions do we bury our heads in the sand or do we try and find a meaningful solution
Derek
Richard how can you say that? The reason there are so many lions in enclosures is because of your support for Captive Bread Lion hunting!

Richard
Negative sir
Derek
What do you mean negative, if there wasn't hunting why would people have started these breeding facilities?
Richard
SA'S game ranching model has gone from 3 farms in the 1960's to over 9000 farms and it's because of the value we give to wildlife - take that value away and we decimate populations.
Derek
All I want you to acknowledge is that Captive bred lion hunting is damaging the image of the country?
Richard
I will not acknowledge that sir because its factually incorrect

LINK
With the country's image at stake internationally the department of environmental affairs has a lot to answer for. We had a confirmed appointment and sent them a list of the questions we would ask, but within hours they cancelled with absolutely no explanation.

Commentary twelve
SAPA is the predator association of lion breeders that make their money from hunting hand raised lions, and slaughtering their lions to sell to the bone trade. We wanted to ask if the minister lets SAPA influence government policy.

Will Travers
SAPA is an influential voice. It seems definitely to have the ear of Minister Molewa

Commentary thirteen
Several members of SAPA's recent leadership are not without controversy. For example, it's president is Kirsten Nematandani, banned for five years by FIFA, for match fixing.

Another former council member is Marnus Steyl, a professional hunter who was charged alongside Thai national Chumlong Lemtongthai in what was to become one of South Africa's most publicized rhino horn smuggling cases. Charges against Steyl were later withdrawn. But surely the minister should distance herself from SAPA, when some of its members have such unsavoury links?

Will Travers
What seems strange is that it seems to be of a lesser concern to the government!

Commentary fourteen
Posing as tourists we visited Boskoppie, a lion breeding farm in the Free state

Up sound

There are over a 100 big cats here, including jaguars leopards and tigers. The owner Piet Swart, we were told by a source, is involved in the bone trade. When we phoned him this week to ask what happens to all his lions, this was his response

Up sound: Piet Swart slams the phone down on Tony Beamish

In 2010 Swart told Carte Blanche he could provide lions for a hunt.

Pieter Swart
Young males, two years, two and a half years old I can get for you. They will be ready for hunting in about a year or a year and two three months.

Commentary fifteen
The NSPCA are seldom welcomed onto these 200 lion breeding farms. Their photos' show lions undernourished, dirty drinking water and no shelter, but the permits issued by provincial nature conservation mean no matter the conditions the breeders are considered legal. The NSPCA'S Marcelle Meredith

Marcelle
They take no cognisance of the welfare of those animals and there is no welfare on the permit

Commentary sixteen
Now the NSPCA have asked the courts to review the minister's decision to legally export 800 lion skeletons. The NSPCA is also puzzled that the department of environment is working against them, when the NSPCA's mandate is precisely to ensure the welfare of the lions

Marcelle
we have two Departments, DEA and the DAFF, and neither one of them know who is supposed to be doing their job. The one just passes the buck from the one to the other!

Commentary seventeen
This effectively leaves the welfare of the lions to the hunters from PHASA and their associates at SAPA.

Richard York PHASA
The type of captive bred lion hunting that we as PHASA endorse is the hunting on 8 accredited SAPA ranches- which is a group of dedicated lion breeders that have put a higher standard …
Derek
Only eight?!
Richard York
At this moment only eight.
Derek
Where does that leave the other 192 and all of those thousands of lions?
Richard
At the moment we are trying to set a standard for them to improve themselves upon - what is very important for PHASA is animal welfare.
Derek
But you are covering such a small percentage of the lion breeders. Eight?
Richard
Small change happens in small increments. We need to start somewhere

Commentary eighteen
If it's even possible, the lions now face a more brutal end. America recently banned the importation of captive bred trophy's which has led to a decline in hunting

Paul Stones
At the end of the day there has got to be an end product, the hunting side is dwindling, of that there is no debate, if there are only 800 permits available, what happens to the other 90% of the lions running around?

Commentary nineteen
This lion is being harvested for its bones and legally a vet must euthenase it. But Carte Blanche has been shown horrible footage of lions piled onto a bakkie and shot, then skinned in a warehouse full of other lion bones. The breeders, says our source are illegally exporting far more than their 800 skeleton quota

Derek
What happens to the thousands of cubs and young lions now that there is a decline in hunting and only 800 permits for lion bone exports?
Richard
We need to have a look at the utilization of those lions. Its vital that we figure out a way to utilize them sustainably
Derek
But what are you doing as PHASA?
Richard
As PHASA it is not currently our mandate sir, we represent the hunters.
Derek
So your mandate is to support captive bred hunting but not to monitor it?
Richard
We do monitor it from a certain aspect yes
Derek
How many of the 192 facilities have you been to?
Richard
Our mission at the moment is on the 8 accredited farms, to create in line with our policies

Commentary Seventeen
The Born Free report concludes with some alarming facts. The DEA has no national database of lions in captivity and instead relies on statistics from SAPA. Born Free also questions why, in the light of overwhelming opposition does the DEA still persist in allowing captive breeding of lions and lion bone exports

THE END In at 01 00 00
Out at 13 30
Promo one in at 14 00, Promo two in at 14 30, promo three in at 15 00

PROMO ONE 10 Seconds
Around 7000 lions are being bred for the bullet by the captive lion breeders. A new report by the Born Free Foundation examines governments role in this industry.

PROMO TWO
Captive bred lion hunting has split the South African hunting industry

Derek
All I want you to acknowledge is that Captive bred lion hunting
Richard
I will not acknowledge that sir because its factually incorrect

PROMO THREE 15 00
Commentary
The Born Free Foundation calls on South Africa to end captive lion breeding

Will Travers
The captive breeding industry in SA doesn't really happen in any other country

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A new report on the lion bone industry exposes just how the department is enabling the cruel killing of our lions for profit
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Hi profile good interviews, and hopefully good confrontations
metadata.Summary: Only 20 000 wild lions remain across the entire African continent. An estimated 8000 of those lions are unashamedly exploited for profit in a cruel and hidden multimillion dollar business right under our noses in the Free State and the North West province. Carte Blanche first exposed the canned hunting business to South Africans in 1997. Twenty years later that industry has given way to a darker, crueler industry - the trading of thousands of lion skeletons, by farmers, Chinese middlemen and exporters and enabled by the DEA, under the leadership of Edna Molewa. In 2017, the South African Government issued an export quota of 800 lion skeletons from captive bred lions, but our sources have told us that thousands more are being exported to Vietnam, China and Laos. By making the trade in lion bones legal, the illegal trade is made easier.
metadata.Further information: South Africa is now the world's largest legal exporter of lion bones and skeletons. Between 2008 and 2015, the country declared exports of more than 5,000 lion skeletons and a large quantity of bones. The buyers and countries to which these products are destined have strong associations with wildlife trafficking. In a new report we track the associations between notorious rhino horn and wildlife smugglers and the lion bone industry and also show an association between this industry and the burgeoning donkey skin industry. According to written answers to questions in parliament, the first legal trade in lion bones and skeleton from South Africa began in 2008 when lion bones began to be used as a substitute for tiger bones in expensive fortifying "wine" and other medicinal products in some Far Eastern communities. Lion bones are sometimes substituted for tiger bones without the knowledge of users. The DEA has repeatedly stated that it believes the breeding of lions in captivity for hunting and trade in skeletons and bones, as a byproduct of hunting, is compatible with the concept of promoting the "Green Economy". However, it acknowledges that it is unable to demonstrate any conservation value from captive lion breeding. The department also acknowledges that it has no scientific evidence to demonstrate that the trade in bones from captive-bred lions will in fact protect wild lions in Africa or tigers in Asia. Several people well connected within the South African hunting industry have indicated in recent interviews with researchers that the price at "the breeding-farm gate" had increased significantly and R30,000 - R50,000 a skeleton is now the going price depending on the size. "The prices have increased a lot since 2013 and some guys are making big money, particularly if the skeleton comes from a lion that someone has already paid to hunt," one professional hunter, who asked not to be named in this report, said during an interview with a researcher. "A trader will pay R50,000 for a big male skeleton with its skull, teeth and claws." So where do the bones go and who is driving the trade? Carte Blanche goes to those named in the report for comment, speaks to international conservation figure Will Travers, the hunters condemning the trade and the Minister of Tourism Mr Derek Hanekom. We also take on the Minister of Environment Edna Molewa whose department is enabling this shocking practice.
